Wednesday. At the park, his cousin Kashish called, "Come play cricket!" Raghav stayed on the swing. "Nobody ever chooses me. I never win anything. Why bother?" Kashish said, "You won the chess thing last month." "That doesn't count."

passage:
Thursday
Mock exam tomorrow and my brain is already saying the usual thing: you always freeze. Every single time.
Himani told me to test it instead of believing it. So here goes. Times I froze: the Class 12 physics board paper, the first-year maths mid-sem, the viva in March.
Times I did NOT freeze: the chemistry mid-sem (got 38/40), the English presentation, the second maths test, the lab exam in April.
Huh. That's four against three. So "always" is wrong.
What was different when I didn't freeze? I'd slept properly. I'd done a full practice paper under a timer. And I started with the question I knew best, not question one.
When I froze, I'd stayed up late and started with question one no matter what.
So tomorrow: sleep by 11. Start with the easiest question.
Tarun

qa.q: What did Tarun score in the chemistry mid-sem?
qa.a: Tarun got 38/40.

qa.a: Tarun feels anxious, with the old voice saying "you always freeze", and becomes steadier after finding four times of not freezing.

qa.q: What did listing the counter-examples show Tarun to work on?
qa.a: That sleep, timed practice and starting with the easiest question made a difference, so those became tomorrow's plan.

qa.q: How might Himani feel on seeing this list?
qa.a: Himani would probably feel pleased and encouraged that testing the belief worked better than just believing it.

grounding: A student who believes they always freeze in exams lists times they didn't and what was different, loosening the rule and finding what to work on.
